title: Did Shakespeare really write all that stuff?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Shakespeare authorship question: whether William Shakespeare of Stratford-upon-Avon wrote the plays attributed to him. They cover what documentary records show about his life (birth, family, schooling, marriage to Anne Hathaway, the lost years, the Groatsworth of Wit "upstart crow" line, his will, tombstone curse, bust and possible sack-of-grain/pillow controversy, First Folio and Ben Jonson's "Swan of Avon" tribute). They then discuss anti-Stratfordian candidates including Delia Bacon and Francis Bacon, Edward de Vere (Oxfordian theory), Christopher Marlowe, Mary Sidney Herbert and Amelia Bassano (including a debunked viral meme), the stigma of print and women-authorship theories, the 1987 C-SPAN mock Supreme Court trial, and pro-Stratford counterarguments. The episode closes with a listener email about squid and a sign-off.

entities.name: Edward de Vere, 17th Earl of Oxford

segments.title: Opening banter and framing the authorship question
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode as denser than expected, note they are agnostic on the question, and frame it as whether the Stratford man William Shakespeare wrote the plays attributed to him, with dozens of proposed candidates over time.

segments.title: Shakespeare's early life and education
segments.summary: The hosts establish that Shakespeare existed and describe his middle-class family, his glover father who became a town official, and his likely schooling at the Stratford grammar school until about thirteen, with the caveat that his education is inferred rather than documented.

segments.title: Marriage, family and the lost years
segments.summary: They cover Shakespeare's marriage to Anne Hathaway, their children including twins Hamnet and Judith, Hamnet's death at eleven, and the roughly seven-year gap in the records before he appears in London. They note that the surviving records are mostly lawsuits, mortgages and banking documents.

segments.title: Documentary evidence: Groatsworth, will, tombstone
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Robert Greene pamphlet Groatsworth of Wit and its 'upstart crow' line, the Stratford house excavations, Shakespeare's 1616 will with no mention of manuscripts or books, and the tombstone curse that does not name him, and how each is read differently by both sides.

segments.title: Why records are sparse and the Atlantic article
segments.summary: They explain that few personal papers survive because the Shakespeare family line ended with his granddaughter, unlike other writers whose family homes preserved papers, and mention musical references in the plays and the Atlantic deep-dive article by Elizabeth Winkler.

segments.title: Spelling variations and elitism argument
segments.summary: The hosts dismiss the many spellings of Shakespeare's name as an era-typical issue and the 'WILLM shack P' abbreviation joke, then discuss the elitism underlying anti-Stratfordian arguments, such as the plays' knowledge of Italy and foreign courts, and the point that the case is really a compliment to the plays.

segments.title: The Stratford bust and the sack of grain debate
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the effigy bust in the Stratford church, whether it was made in life or after death, Professor Orlan's argument that it was likely commissioned while he was alive, and the dispute over whether the cushion beneath the hands is a pillow or a sack of grain. They also note the missing quill and the reported missing skull.

segments.title: First Folio, Ben Jonson and Delia Bacon
segments.summary: They cover the First Folio and Ben Jonson's tribute calling Shakespeare the Swan of Avon, and the rival reading that Jonson was being insincere. They then introduce Delia Bacon, the American writer who first publicly doubted Shakespeare and proposed Francis Bacon and Walter Raleigh, her reliance on the plays and visits to the tomb, and Ralph Waldo Emerson's sponsorship.

segments.title: Break and transition on Delia Bacon's legacy
segments.summary: Brief break, followed by discussion of Delia Bacon's close-reading method, her book The Philosophy of the Plays of Shakespeare Unfolded, and the James Wilmot documents later suspected of forgery.

segments.title: Oxfordian and Derby theories, Marlowe, and women authors
segments.summary: They describe the Oxfordian theory favoring Edward de Vere, the Derby theory and the dedicated narrative poems, and the Marlowe faked-death theory, which they find unlikely. They then cover theories that women such as Mary Sidney Herbert and Amelia Bassano wrote the plays, including a viral misleading meme about Bassano.

segments.title: 1987 mock trial, pro-Stratford evidence and wrap-up
segments.summary: They describe the 1987 C-SPAN mock trial with three Supreme Court justices that went two to one for Shakespeare of Stratford, then cover pro-Stratford evidence such as Venus and Adonis, Richard Field, contemporaneous critics, the coat of arms and William Camden's praise. They close by noting the debate is largely a matter of belief.

segments.title: Listener mail on eating squid
segments.summary: A listener email from Stephen in Kagoshima, Japan argues squid deserve to be eaten because they cannibalize their own eggs and hatchlings, and warns against eating raw squid.
